OSHA 29 CFR 1910.213 sets point-of-operation guarding rules for saws, jointers, shapers and similar machines. This confirms the task means hands-on operation of dangerous machinery. It does not require a licensed person to sign off.

O*NET lists reading blueprints, drawings or written specifications to work out pattern sizes, shapes and machine setups as a core task for wood patternmakers. The other core duties are physical: laying out stock, running bandsaws and lathes, assembling and measuring.

AI tools and research systems can already pull dimensions and tolerances from engineering drawings automatically. Reported accuracy is about 81% for a research pipeline and 90-95% in vendor claims, so a human still needs to check the output. The search found no tool built for foundry pattern allowances such as shrinkage, draft or core prints.
None of the career sources mention a license or certification requirement for wood patternmakers. Training is a high school diploma or a post-secondary certificate, plus apprenticeship.

Dedicated sawmill scanners such as Lucidyne, Weinig CombiScan and FinScan use deep learning with cameras, lasers and x-ray to find defects and grade lumber. They are fixed industrial machines with sensors, not general software AI agents. In one study they were more accurate than human line graders.

A Microtec Goldeneye scanner with the GradeView algorithm graded 9,454 hardwood boards with 92% grade accuracy. Most of its errors came from board geometry, which means the board has to be physically measured and handled.

Accredited agencies own the grade stamps and run spot checks on mills. Certified graders or machine grading apply the stamps, but this applies to official grade stamping, not to an operator's routine inspection of stock at the saw.

Machines that scan for defects and optimize cuts already find flaws, work out the best cuts from a cut list and send them to a CNC crosscut saw. These are dedicated mill machines, not software agents, and the work still happens at the physical stock.
The TigerSaw1000 reads cut lists, but someone still marks defects on the board in crayon. This shows that measuring and marking stock is hands-on work at the board.

The software step, matching order data against flaw locations to produce cut lines, is the only part a software-only agent could help with. The physical measuring and marking stays with a person or a machine.

Older cutting machines were run by hand, with operators working close to moving parts. PLC-based control systems are built to replace that manual operation, but they are fixed machine controllers, not software agents.

On a PLC/HMI panel-cutting line, the operator enters the panel count and size and starts the cycle at a control screen on the machine. The controller then secures the panel, makes the cut and returns. Starting the machine still happens at the machine.
Recent retrofits of cutting machines add safety door bars and safety switches on the protective shields, so starting and running the machine depends on a person at the guarded machine.

Knife positioning on slitters is automated by PLC and touch-screen systems that use machine actuators and stored job recipes. This is factory hardware, not something an AI agent controls. Fitting the blades still takes physical work: knife holders are usually repositioned and clamped by hand.

In the Computaslit system, the operator enters slit widths or recalls a saved recipe, and an electric actuator moves the knives into position. Software can help choose settings from the specifications, but a person still mounts the blades, rollers and templates.
The knife holders mount on a dovetail support bar and are normally moved and clamped by hand. Installing components with hand tools needs a physical presence that a software-only agent does not have.
MES application servers are set up to print production labels on Zebra printers, so the ticket content can be generated from system data without anyone filling it in by hand.
In this production-operator posting, the operator prints pallet tickets, applies them and checks that the information is correct. Putting the ticket on the product is physical work.
On an extrusion line, the operator checks that the labels match the shift schedule's lot, color and denier, and applies a stamped label to each finished package by hand.

O*NET 51-9124.00 lists 'Operate auxiliary machines or equipment used in coating or painting processes' as a supplemental task. The occupation's core tasks are hands-on: positioning spray guns, adjusting dials and valves, and disposing of hazardous waste.

Paint-line auxiliaries such as conveyors, ovens, pumps and paint circuits are run by on-site PLC/HMI control systems with recipe management and diagnostics. These systems are operated by shop-floor staff, not by general-purpose AI agents, and an alert goes to a human supervisor when a correction limit is reached.

Even where remote assistance is possible over an Ethernet-connected HMI, the work is still done at the machine: loading, starting, adjusting and clearing it. Plant control networks are normally closed to outside software agents.

Run-to-run control takes metrology results after each wafer step and automatically calculates parameter changes for the next wafer. Software already does much of the routine monitoring and adjustment.

AI/ML run-to-run control has been shown in closed-loop deposition and can outperform classic APC for some processes. Its effectiveness still depends on model quality and measurement latency, so engineers and technicians handle exceptions and retune.
A typical fab has about 2500 on-line SPC charts, and manual over-adjustment can make processes oscillate. Fabs therefore depend on automated factory-wide control systems.
Automated part labeling relies on software that generates label data and sends it to peripheral label devices, so the agent's piece is digital: preparing label content and print jobs.
Automated part marking for traceability is done by robotic or fixed laser and dot-peen hardware, which is industrial automation, not a software-only AI agent.
Marking data can be pulled straight from ERP/SAP/MES systems, which is the sub-step an AI agent could speed up. Physically marking, tagging and handling the parts still needs a person or a machine.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), the employer must certify each powered lift truck operator after formal instruction, hands-on practical training and an in-person evaluation in the workplace. The forklift part of the task is done by a trained, certified human operator, and federal law bars anyone under 18 from operating these trucks in non-agricultural jobs.

Moving material around warehouses without a human is done by physical robots (AMRs) run by fleet orchestration software. A software-only agent with no body cannot carry, push or drive loads. At most it could help with digital side steps such as reading a move ticket in the WMS or planning a route.

Warehouse robotics software assigns tasks, plans paths and manages charging for physical robots that connect to WMS/ERP systems. The movement itself still needs physical hardware, not just a language-model agent.

O*NET lists 'Break up defective products for reprocessing' as a task for Helpers--Production Workers (51-9198.00). It is manual work on the factory floor: breaking, crushing or taking apart rejected goods by hand or with hand tools so they can be reprocessed.
Several other hands-on production jobs list the same task, such as 51-9111.00, 51-4071.00 and 51-9161.00. This confirms it is shop-floor physical work and not a digital or information task.
Software alone can't do this task. An agent with no robotics could at most help with minor paperwork, such as logging scrap or reprocessing records, which is not a substantial part of the task.

Tank truck seals are one-use tamper-evident devices put on valves, hatches and closures by hand after loading. Cable seals with metal locking bodies are recommended for valve outlets, so the work is hands-on at the vehicle.
Rail tankers and tank trucks normally have a place on the valve, or on the box covering it, where a seal such as a strap seal is attached by hand.
Bottom outlet valves are mechanical parts on the tank car. Their inspection and closure are physical work done on the car itself.

OSHA 1910.269 applies to line-clearance tree trimming. It includes training (paragraph b) and job-briefing requirements, which an employer and a person in charge on site must meet. The search results did not give the exact wording of the training paragraph.

Arborist software such as ArboStar and Arbster handles crew scheduling, task assignment, risk-assessment forms and gear-inspection tracking. It supports supervision but does not oversee climbers or train them in the field.
GoCanvas form templates record safety meetings and training on PPE, pruning near power lines and climbing safety. They cover the paperwork side of training, not hands-on teaching.
Tree trimmers do the work by climbing with arborist gear or from aerial trucks. They cut with saws, lower the cut sections with ropes and feed a chipper. All of it is physical work done on site.
Most US states require workers who apply pesticides and fertilizers to hold a licence, which usually means passing a test.

Drone pruning near power lines (UK Power Networks' Aero Prune, Dec 2025 to Sep 2026) is still a trial that needs hardware, not a software agent. It is not a commercial product that software alone could run.
Employer groundperson job listings describe this work as raking and leaf-blowing the job site and cleaning up debris on site: hands-on work that has to be done in person.
Crew-member duties include raking, sweeping and blowing, and gathering brush, limbs and logs and carrying them to the chipping area. All of this is manual work on site.
O*NET lists collecting debris into piles and loading it onto trucks as tasks for Tree Trimmers and Pruners (37-3013.00). Nothing digital in the task could be done by a software agent.

Chemical tree treatments need a state pesticide applicator license in general. For example, Washington's WSDA Commercial Pesticide Applicator license covers anyone applying pesticides on another person's land. In Connecticut, an arborist license also makes the holder a supervisory pesticide applicator.

Software calculators such as Toro's Sprayer Calibration Tool already handle tank-mix, nozzle-selection and application-rate math. This is the only digital part of the task. The actual mixing, calibration runs and spraying are done by hand with physical equipment in the field.

Connecticut requires a state arborist license for anyone advertising or contracting arboriculture work, and that license carries pesticide applicator responsibility. A licensed human has to perform or supervise the application.
Splitting is done by hand: you set an axe or wedge along the grain, hit it with a sledgehammer, then drive wedges into the crack. A software-only agent cannot do any of this.

The work means swinging a maul or sledge, judging knots and how thick the log is, and adding wedges as needed. It takes physical effort and carries a risk of injury, which is why a person has to be there.
Specialized tools like starter wedges and quartering wedges are physical devices that a person still has to drive into the wood.

In 2025, major retailers and AI companies launched agentic shopping assistants. Amazon's Rufus now buys products automatically, and ChatGPT added checkout. These tools find out what a shopper needs and suggest specific products without a human involved.
Reported uses of AI agents in consumer retail include personalized product recommendations. BCG reports a 5–15% conversion lift for retailers that run their own AI agents.

Agentic shopping tools moved from comparing products to recommending and buying them for the shopper. However, demonstrators and product promoters usually work in person, in stores or at events. There they read the customer and persuade face to face, which an agent cannot do without a body. No licence or legal sign-off is required for the task.

Google's Try On tool, launched in June 2026, lets a user upload a photo and generates an image of clothing and accessories on that person. It only produces images. It cannot put real garments on a body.

Virtual try-on APIs such as FLUX Virtual Try-On Pro take a person image, a garment and a styling instruction (for example tucked in or layered). They can suggest styling for the accessory-selection part of the task, but a human model still has to physically put on the garments.
One 2026 vendor ranking covers virtual try-on tools for clothing, accessories and makeup. All of them work on images or video for previews and shopping. None of them dress a person.

Voice agent lets a field rep dictate line items in front of a customer; the system creates the ERP order with the correct pricing tier, confirms totals and queues it for submission, with credit-limit and approval rules and escalation of exceptions to people (vendor claim).
Voice-to-CRM tools turn field reps' voice recordings into structured entries in Salesforce, HubSpot, Microsoft Dynamics and other CRMs (vendor claim).

A proof of concept for a Microsoft Dynamics 365 client used an AI agent to read order emails and attachments, validate them and post orders to the ERP, with a human customer-service rep approving each order; no results were reported.

Salesforce's Prospecting Agent runs in the background, takes plain-language instructions about the target profile, and produces a ranked list of accounts and contacts. A customer reports that 60% of its North American pipeline was built autonomously.

Lead-list agents filter prospects by industry, size, location and job title, and remove duplicates already in the CRM. These tools are built for B2B contact databases, not household-level data for door-to-door territories.
AI SDR products such as Artisan's Ava and HubSpot's Prospecting Agent build prospect lists on their own. Reviewers still advise human supervision because list quality varies.

Tank-mix apps already calculate product amounts per load and the correct mixing order. These are only the planning sub-steps; a person still has to measure, mix and pour the material into the machine.
Farm-management platforms such as Traction include a tank mix calculator linked to work orders that are assigned to operators, so the AI can help with planning but not with the physical handling.

Under federal rules, mixing and loading restricted-use pesticides counts as 'use'. It must be done by a certified applicator, or by trained workers under direct supervision, and some labels require the certified applicator to be physically present.
