evidence.fact: Hitching an implement is hands-on work on the machine itself: stopping the engine, leveling the lower links, setting the control valve to float, and making the PTO, hydraulic and lighting connections by hand. A software-only agent cannot do any of these steps. At most it can look up the procedure in a manual.

Even an automatic quick-hitch system that coupled the PTO and hydraulics as the tractor backed in was a mechanical device, not AI software, and it is no longer produced. Attaching implements still depends on physical tools and a person to handle them.

Dedicated optical sorting machines (cameras plus air-ejector valves) reject rotten produce on belt lines. This is automation built into the machine hardware, not something a software-only AI agent can do.
AI vision reject separators work as physical machines on potato and onion lines. Removing the product needs mechanical action on the conveyor.
AI-powered optical sorting requires installing dedicated sorting hardware to separate rejected material from accepted produce.

Camera-based systems can score dairy cow body condition, mobility (lameness) and weight automatically, and in real-world tests did as well as or better than manual scoring. This only works where the cameras are installed on the farm.
In June 2026, SLU released an AI mobile app that measures and weighs dairy cows to help assess health and welfare. A person still has to be with the animal to capture the images.

Commercial vision products such as COW-AI claim real-time lameness scoring (1 to 5) and body condition scoring. These are vendor claims, so the AI analysis supports the on-farm hands-on exam (handling, palpation, temperature checks) rather than replacing it.

OSHA logging rules (29 CFR 1910.266(h)) require planning and clearing an escape path before felling, then moving a safe distance away on it once the back cut is made. This is physical, on-site work by the faller.

OSHA's Logging eTool checklist lists chain saw work practices under 1910.266(e)(2) that include retreating with the saw and moving with a running chain saw. These are hands-on saw handling tasks at the stump.
Industry felling-safety guidance says the sawyer must plan two retreat routes to use when the cut tree starts to fall. The task depends on the person being physically present at the tree.

OSHA's logging guidance has the feller size and place the hinge, face cut and back cut on site, judging the tree's lean, diameter and condition. Wedges go into the back cut to fell against back lean, and timing them depends on how the tree is moving in real time.
Automated felling guidance (scanning a tree, estimating its center of gravity and rating fall directions) exists only as a patent concept, not a shipping product.
Research smartphone apps can estimate trunk diameter and lean direction from a photo, which could help a human decide, but they don't plan the cuts or wedges.

Oregon OSHA requires the hazard area around an unattended lodged or partly cut tree to be marked with hazard identification ribbon, and only qualified workers may fall danger trees. The ribbon must be bright orange and marked 'Danger' or with a skull and crossbones. Every cutter has to carry it.
California 8 CCR 6275(f) requires a qualified person to flag the hazardous area around an unattended lodged tree with warning tape or ribbon at the logging site.

Australian bushfire guidance says crews mark the zone around a dangerous tree on site with surveyor's tape or danger tape. The marked zone must be at least as large as the tree's height, so a person has to judge it on the ground and tie the tape by hand.
Automated rebar tying exists only as physical robotics. TyBot is a gantry robot on rails that finds rebar intersections and ties them with a robotic arm, and the reference technology excludes robots.
Even the robot needs a worker to supervise it, and it mainly pays off on large bridge decks and long rectangular slabs. Spacing and tying rods in forms is hands-on manual work done on site.

TyBot ties about 1,100 to 1,200 intersections per hour on bridge decks. A software agent cannot do any of the physical spacing or tying. At most it can help read blueprints or bar schedules, which is a small share of the time.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451(f)(7), scaffolds may only be erected, moved, dismantled or altered under the supervision and direction of a competent person. A competent person must also judge foundation adequacy and inspect the scaffold before each shift. This is hands-on work done on site by people.

Scaffold design software such as Avontus Scaffold Designer, scaffmax and CerTus can automate layouts, parts lists and assembly plans. It does not do the physical erection, which is the core of this helper task.
scaffmax generates scaffolding automatically wall by wall on 3D building models and produces parts lists, so only a small planning sub-step could be done in software.

Hanging a chain-link gate is all hands-on work. The worker measures and cuts pipe, squares and bolts the frame, fits tension bands and bars, stretches and trims the mesh, mounts the hinges, lifts the gate onto the hinge pins, levels it, and adjusts the latch. This needs wrenches, pliers, cutters and a level, and an AI with no body cannot do it.

The gate is built from manufacturer kits and written instructions. Software can only help by finding instructions or working out cut lengths, such as the opening width minus about 6 inches. That is a very small part of the job.

Fence licensing applies to the business, not to the worker who assembles a gate. One example is California's C13 licence for jobs above a dollar threshold. Some Canadian sources say fence installation is not a regulated trade, so no law requires a human to sign off this task.

The Geismar LRH-5-SP hydraulic rail lifter is run by an operator at each end using local controls for the clamps and jacks. The work is done on site with heavy hydraulic equipment and has no software interface a remote agent could use.

The Unipart rail handler comes with manually operated rail grabs and threaders. Hydraulic control is optional, and radio control is offered as a remote option for an operator who is still on site. None of this is a networked digital system an AI agent could reach.
O*NET lists this task for occupation 47-4061 as pushing controls to close grasping devices on track so it can be raised or moved. It is direct physical operation of equipment on the track.

On a rig, air from an onboard compressor blows cuttings out of the hole. This is part of operating the machine itself. Any automation of the step comes from control systems built into the rig, not from a general-purpose software agent.

Some rigs have built-in autonomous flushing procedures, but a remote operator can override them. Field data from the Telfer mine showed manual drilling cycles were 19% faster than automated ones, so automating this step depends on special rig hardware and controls.

Controlling drill dust takes physical work at the rig, such as keeping dust collectors working and drilling holes wet. Drill operators at the machine get the highest dust exposure, which shows the task has to be done in person.

Commercial diving work in the US, including underwater debris removal, falls under OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart T. The rule requires human divers on site with dive teams, a designated person-in-charge and safety procedures. The work involves hands-on hazards such as cutting, material handling and cleaning.

Minnesota regulators apply the Subpart T commercial diving rules to underwater removal work done on scuba, such as aquatic weed removal. They issued a $730,369 penalty after a diver drowned. This shows the task is physical, in-water work that requires a human.

OSHA guidance describes diver hazards that come from working physically underwater and handling materials there. A software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do this. At most, it could help with paperwork or planning on the side.

Laser alignment systems such as the Easy-Laser XT app and SKF TKSA 51 compute alignment corrections and guide the operator step by step. A person still has to mount the measuring units and physically move, shim and bolt the machine.
SKF TKSA 51 uses a tablet app with a live 3D view of the measuring units to guide alignment of motors, fans and gearboxes. The app only processes readings and does not do the manual adjustment.
Rigger and millwright job postings describe very physical, hands-on work: setting machines with jacks, levels and lasers, building foundations with grout and steel, and lifting heavy loads.
O*NET lists this as a core hands-on task for Electromechanical Equipment Assemblers (51-2023.00), done alongside fastening units with hand and power tools.

Related tasks include measuring tolerances with micrometers and calipers and filing, lapping or buffing parts by hand to fit. This is physical work that a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do. At most it can help by reading blueprints or giving assembly-sequence guidance.
When this work is automated, it is done by robots or fixed automation that assemblers operate or tend, not by digital AI agents. No license or legal sign-off is required for the task.

Velvet is finished by holding steam a few inches from the fabric or steaming it from the back on a pile-down board, then brushing gently in the direction of the nap. Every step is hands-on work with the garment.
Velvet is finished by steaming and hand-brushing the pile with a soft brush, never by ironing. The work needs tactile judgment on a physical fabric.
The machines that steam and brush pile fabrics are physical equipment, so a software-only agent cannot run them.

The task is done by hand. A worker presses ties using pressure, inserted metal forms or rods, and careful hand ironing so the rolled seams don't flatten. An AI agent that works only through software cannot do any substantial part of this.

In the O*NET listing for Pressers, Textile, Garment, and Related Materials (51-6021.00), the tasks are physical work with heated metal forms and hand irons on garments. I couldn't open this page directly because it redirected to O*NET's job-coding help page, so this comes from the search result summary.
Forum posts describe a heated metal 'Nek-Tie Iron' rod that a worker pushes into the tie to dry and press it at the same time. This is hands-on work, and the sources are informal.

The leading end of new fabric is joined to the trailing end of the fabric being processed by stitching transverse seams with a standby hand sewing machine. Someone has to physically line up the fabric and run the machine.
Comatex sells portable chainstitch machines for joining fabric at the entry to dyeing and finishing machines. These are hand-operated physical tools, not software.
Sewing tracks for joining pieces at the entry to finishing machines are mechanical gear that an operator loads and runs on the shop floor.

O*NET lists this as a task of Textile Cutting Machine Setters, Operators, and Tenders. In the occupation's work context, 72% use their hands continually and 73% stand continually, and the role needs finger dexterity and arm-hand steadiness.

Patents show that machine threading is done by hand or with built-in pneumatic and mechanical self-threading devices. Even with automatic threading, an operator still places the yarn end by hand, so the work is physical machinery, not software.
Older textile threading tools, such as hand-operated pumps for pulling yarn through ducts, are manual devices. None of the threading methods found involves a software or AI agent.

Wood bleaching means mixing chemicals (two-part sodium hydroxide/hydrogen peroxide or oxalic acid) and brushing them by hand into the grain with a foam, nylon or scrub brush, then repeating and neutralizing as needed. All of this is physical work an agent without a body cannot do.

Getting an even result depends on judging the wood by eye and hand: testing on a hidden spot, deciding whether to reapply, wiping with vinegar to neutralize, and checking for embedded ferrous metal. Software can only offer step-by-step guidance on these steps.
The main constraints are safety ones (eye protection, gloves, ventilation, non-metal containers). No licence or sign-off by a person is required.

Speedcargo's Amplifi tool creates ULD-level load plans from booked cargo and aircraft type. Its Assemble tool gives ground handlers step-by-step digital build-up plans. Etihad Cargo has these in use in Singapore and is piloting them in Frankfurt, so the planning sub-step is automatable.

AI engines that use 3D spatial analysis and combinatorial optimisation can generate ULD build-up plans covering dimensions, weight, contours and dangerous-goods rules. This claim comes from a vendor explainer, so it is unverified. The physical build-up and placement of cargo is still done by people on the ramp or warehouse floor.

I found no federal certificate that an FAA load supervisor must hold. Load supervision and verification follow operator procedures under AC 120-85, and a 2018 FAA working group only studied certification for special cargo.

Ships are usually controlled from the bridge, the engine control room or locally at the engine. Rules say only one location may control propulsion at a time, and local manual control must stay available if the remote system fails. Bridge control is built-in shipboard automation, not something a general-purpose AI agent can reach.
Vard's SeaQ Remote lets specialized class-approved systems run engines, propellers and thrusters remotely, but only on purpose-built autonomous newbuilds. Ordinary ships do not have it.

STCW and national rules such as 46 CFR 11.329 require a certified engineer to be in charge of an engineering watch, or to be the designated duty engineer when the engine room is periodically unmanned.

Atatus released Watchtower AI RCA in April 2026. The vendor says it finds anomalies and root causes from real traffic patterns without manual thresholds, so the detection and diagnosis steps of performance monitoring are already automated. This is a vendor claim with no independent benchmark.

A Tech Week Singapore 2026 session abstract describes multi-agent AI systems that detect performance regressions in production apps and locate their root causes. It also notes that diagnostics differ by platform, which makes the work hard. This is a conference abstract, not a peer-reviewed study.

A vendor comparison page credits Dynatrace's causal AI root-cause analysis with a 65% cut in MTTR. The figure is not independently verified. The task is done entirely in software, and I found no licence or legal sign-off requirement for monitoring program performance.

A ScreenSkills career guide says AI tools can help hair and makeup departments track continuity across scenes. That is support work like reference photos and notes. Applying makeup to the performer is still done by hand.
The search found no dedicated on-set makeup continuity software that applies makeup. Current AI makeup tools only retouch photos or offer virtual try-on, not physical work on a real face.

Makeup continuity means keeping an actor's look consistent from day to day and shot to shot. A digital agent can check reference images, but someone has to physically apply products and prosthetics to the actor's face.
Chopping tar into small pieces and heating it in kettles is a listed core duty of roofer helpers, along with hoisting tar and materials onto roofs. All of it is physical work done on site.

Running a kettle safely means physical work on site: setting the kettle on firm, level ground, keeping the temperature below the flash point, having a fire extinguisher at hand and putting up barriers to keep the public back.
Utah requires an attendant to stay within 100 feet of the kettle whenever the burner is lit. This is a safety-supervision rule, not a licensing requirement.

O*NET lists this as a Dredge Operator task: directing or helping workers place shore anchors and cables, lay pipe from the dredge to shore, and pump water from pontoons. All of this is hands-on work on the water and at the shoreline.

A leverman job posting says the role includes directing or helping crew members place shore anchors and cables and assemble, position and lay pipe. This is physical rigging work done on site, not work done in software.

Related duties include running power winches, pulling in cables by hand and lowering anchor poles, all done at remote dredging sites. An agent that works only through software has no way to do or directly oversee this work.

A patent for 'personalized chatbots for inmates' describes a server that answers inmate questions from stored data and offers counseling suggestions. This shows that answering routine written requests through tablets or kiosks can be automated in part.
Most prisons forbid inmates from going online. Official AI chatbot use on secure tablets is limited to pilots such as Northeastern's Prison Project, so agents rarely reach the inmate-facing channel.

A 2025 thesis finds that LLM chatbots on prison tablets can support inmates, but deploying them requires careful calibration against institutional constraints. Face-to-face counseling by officers in housing units is still done by humans.

In 2026 TSA put Ace, a Salesforce-built AI agent, on tsa.gov and the myTSA app. Salesforce reports it handles about 100,000 traveler conversations a month and resolves 96% of routine questions without a human. Harder cases go to live staff with an AI-written summary.
Since 2019, TSA's @AskTSA virtual assistant has answered common screening questions automatically around the clock, in English and Spanish. A human team handles complex questions.

Screeners mostly do this task in person at the checkpoint, pointing and guiding people in lines and lanes, often as part of the screening itself. A software-only agent can take over the informational questions through apps, kiosks or chat, but not the face-to-face directing, which needs someone physically there.

In a vendor case study, Ekimetrics' generative-AI ESG Copilot scored a client's existing reporting against about 1,200 CSRD disclosure requirements and recommended fixes for the gaps. The firm says this took 6 weeks instead of 6 months, a figure it reported itself.

Under the CSRD, the board, management and audit committee hold ultimate responsibility for sustainability reporting. The board must approve the management report that contains the sustainability disclosures, so a human still has to sign off on the compliance judgment.

CSRD reporting must get third-party limited assurance, which requires traceable audit trails. AI-generated metrics make that verification harder, so a human needs to review the AI's output before it is used.

Power-plant maintenance software (CMMS) vendors say their products set reorder points from supplier lead times and past usage, and create purchase orders automatically when stock falls below those points. These are vendor claims and have not been checked independently.
Maintenance software already handles safety stock, reorder points and automated purchase requests. AI adds changing reorder levels based on usage trends and how reliable each supplier is.

Vendor pages describe AI that predicts delivery delays, builds parts kits for planned shutdowns and flags obsolete stock. People still have to count stock on site, receive and inspect deliveries, and approve spending on critical spares. No law or licence requires a human to manage inventory.

A study used machine learning on SCADA data from a biomass power plant. An Isolation Forest flagged anomalies and a Random Forest sorted operating states at about 96% accuracy. The data covered only one 24-hour period at one plant.

A peer-reviewed study pulled startup, shutdown and failure events from short operator log entries with F1 scores of 80-92%. Specialised NLP beat generative AI used alone, so log review can be automated but still needs a human to check it.
Vendors are selling agentic AI and copilots that search historians, CMMS data and shift logbooks and produce ranked alerts and work orders. Their performance claims are not independently checked.

Vendor tools say they can turn compliance policy documents into structured, interactive courses with auto-generated quizzes and role-based learning paths. This covers the content design and e-learning delivery sub-steps.
AI voice and chat agents are being pitched for interactive compliance training tailored to each employee's role and risk exposure. Most of this evidence is vendor marketing, not independent testing.

The DOJ guidance on corporate compliance programs judges training by risk-based design and measured effectiveness. It does not require live or human-delivered training. Even so, human review of AI-written content and live facilitation still help with credibility and with leadership setting the tone.

Vendor sources (unverified marketing) say 2026 TMS platforms embed AI agents. Trimble's dispatch optimization has agents across seven modules, and project44 offers an Intelligent TMS. These agents optimize routing and load consolidation and act on the results, not just recommend.

Agent-based load planning re-plans routes and consolidation against capacity, hours-of-service, traffic and weather limits. Agents handle routine cases and pass unusual ones to human operators, so a human still reviews strategic and exception decisions.

A TMS overview credits route optimization, load consolidation and carrier rate optimization with 5-15% lower transport costs (figure not independently sourced). This is software work with no physical step and no licensing or sign-off requirement found.

The COSO/ACFE Fraud Risk Management Guide sets out a structured fraud risk assessment: find fraud schemes, then judge their likelihood and impact against existing controls. Much of that structured work can be done with software and documents, though it still needs judgment about incentives, opportunities and rationalizations.

Fraud risk assessments now need to cover AI-enabled methods such as fabricated documents and fake approval requests. The UK's 'failure to prevent fraud' rule has applied to large organisations since September 2025. It makes the organisation accountable for its controls, but it does not require a licensed person to carry out the assessment.

The CFE Code of Professional Standards is an ethics code that individual fraud examiners apply to their own cases. It does not legally require a licensed human to perform or sign a fraud risk assessment.

Nokia's Gemini-powered agents (triage, anomaly reasoner, action reasoner) are said to cut telecom troubleshooting time by 50-80% for some issues. Operators still approve critical actions, and only low-risk cases run in closed loop.
TeamViewer's Tia agent, launched in November 2025, combines remote connectivity with finding and fixing IT and device problems on its own, which covers remote diagnosis and software fixes.
Agentic service desks handle routine L1 tickets through system APIs and pass non-routine issues to humans. Hardware faults that need on-site work are still done by people.

Saama's SDTM-RAG uses several AI agents to map source fields to SDTM domains and variables, check the mappings, and write SAS or R code. In vendor-reported pilots, about 75% of mappings were generated automatically, with roughly 70% accuracy. Users still approve or reject each suggested mapping.
A PharmaSUG 2026 paper argues that AI alone cannot resolve sponsor conventions or ambiguous metadata. It recommends combining deterministic rules with review by a programmer.

Under 21 CFR Part 11 (FDA rules on electronic records), clinical electronic records must run on validated systems with audit trails. Each change has to be traceable to an identified user, so a qualified human typically reviews and accepts formatted datasets before use.

ICH Q14 and USP <1220> frame the work as lifecycle management: set an analytical target profile, find critical method parameters, monitor performance continuously and improve. Much of this means analysing data and documents, which an agent can do from a goal: reviewing SOPs and validation reports, trending system-suitability and OOS data, searching the literature and drafting improvement proposals. Vendor tools such as ACD/Labs AutoChrom already digitise method development.

Under GMP, the quality unit is responsible for approving procedures and results, and lab records must reference method validation data. A qualified human must therefore approve and sign off on proposed method changes. Checking a proposed improvement also needs bench experiments in the physical lab.

Uptake of Q14's enhanced, data-driven tools is still low, at about 19% in an ISPE poll. Method data usually sits in LIMS and chromatography data systems that an agent may not be able to reach. Search results showed no autonomous AI agent doing regulated method evaluation from start to finish.
Pre-procedure room setup is hands-on work: setting up the endoscope and video tower, laying out supplies and getting specimen-management supplies ready.
Techs pick the correct endoscope and run a physical quality-control check on it before each procedure.

Techs choose the equipment, supplies and instruments for each procedure based on the procedure type and the patient's needs. An agent could only help with the planning side, such as drafting checklists from the schedule or preference cards.

SLP documentation tools such as Ambiki's Tenalog record and transcribe session audio and produce SOAP notes. They also pull out structured data for progress tracking, analyse errors and draft progress summaries. That covers much of the compiling and documentation work.

SLPAs collect performance data during therapy sessions and prepare records under the direction of a supervising SLP. Much of the raw data comes from watching client responses live, often in person, and judging each trial and the level of prompting.

ASHA recommends that the supervising SLP regularly review the data for every client the SLPA serves, and the SLP keeps overall responsibility. A human therefore reviews the data, but no rule requires a human to collect or compile it.

Guard-management platforms such as TrackTik, Guardix and SecurityTime already handle scheduling, dispatch, digital post orders, patrol-tour checks, incident reporting, and automated AI calls to guards who are late.
In retail security, AI video analytics run alongside human agents. Humans check the alerts and coordinate dispatch, so people still direct the response on the ground.

Interface Systems reports that interactive remote video monitoring resolved 62.4% of high-priority retail events without police dispatch. This shows that much of the coordination of the response can be done remotely through digital systems.

Under Food Code rules, cleaning is hands-on work. Utensils and equipment must be scraped, washed in detergent, rinsed, sanitized with chemicals or 171°F water, and air dried. Surfaces must be clean to sight and touch, and equipment used with TCS food must be cleaned every 4 hours.

Cleaning automation is built into the machines themselves, with timer-triggered cleaning cycles for the coffee and milk systems. These cycles do not require a software agent, and staff still have to do the manual steps.
Cafe software can only schedule and track maintenance. It cannot do the physical cleaning, so an AI agent's role is limited to checklists and logs.

Square launched an AI voice-ordering kiosk in October 2026. It has payment processing and Square Loyalty built in, so a customer can order and pay for card or wallet transactions with no barista involved.
At a café POS, customers insert, tap or swipe their own cards. For cash, the barista enters the amount handed over and physically gives back the change, which software alone cannot do.
Shared tap-to-pay terminals can put a payment on the wrong tab, so a person still has to watch over payment handling in a busy shop.

Cameras and AI mounted on collection trucks, from vendors like Prairie Robotics, automatically detect contamination, overfilled carts and bins that weren't set out. They send photos and feedback to residents. More than 20 North American cities use them, so the monitoring and notification steps can be automated.
Coordinator job descriptions include field inspections of drop-off sites and facilities, and investigating and documenting ordinance violations. These steps need someone physically on site.

Some postings say coordinators issue violation notices and work with compliance departments on code violations and illegal dumping. These are enforcement steps where a human with authority has to act.

Commercial AI and geospatial platforms (e.g., Solonic on ArcGIS) and open planning tools (e.g., WaPla) already model waste flows, costs and emissions, simulate operations and redesign collection systems, which covers the main analytical sub-steps of program design.

Planning tools such as WaPla map municipal waste flows and estimate greenhouse gas emissions and costs per process, which supports scenario design for reduction, recycling, composting and disposal programs.

US state statutes require solid waste management plans to go through public comment periods and hearings, be adopted by local governing bodies and be approved by a state agency, so stakeholder engagement and human adoption stay essential. A licensed professional's signature is not typically required.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l) says only trained operators whom the employer has certified and authorized may run forklifts and other powered industrial trucks. Training includes hands-on practice and an evaluation in the workplace.

Autonomous forklifts (for example DHL's 15 units) are robots with LIDAR and camera hardware, not software-only agents. The search found no recycling facility using them, so the reference technology, which has no body, cannot move materials itself.
Recycling facilities are messy, unpredictable places where items arrive overlapping and in random positions, which makes physical handling hard to automate.

Dillon Consulting and Toronto Metropolitan University are building an AI system that moves site-visit data into pre-formatted Word templates and writes report text from past reports. They aim to automate 75–80% of the energy audit report. This is a project description, not a finished product.

Existing audit tools already run ASHRAE Level 1–3 analyses and produce standardized reports automatically: OptiMiser Commercial does measure analysis and reporting, and simuwatt/NREL generates standardized reports. Neither is described as AI-driven. The report-writing part of the task is digital, but the input data comes from physical site visits.

NYC Department of Buildings rules for Local Law 87 limit who can submit Energy Efficiency Reports to Registered Design Professionals. A human therefore has to certify and sign the report, though secondary sources disagree on the exact qualifications.

AI dosing guidance tools such as UpToDate Expert AI exist in 2026. They are built to keep a clinician in the loop, and hallucination in unusual dosing cases is seen as a high risk. I found no autonomous prescribing systems in use.
Clinical decision support tools built into the EHR read current medications and lab results and return dosing and interaction suggestions. A clinician still approves any change.
State law and board rules set who may prescribe, and only licensed people such as nurse practitioners and physicians qualify. Some states require a physician to cosign or work under protocols.
Alma Analytics reports can be exported to CSV, Excel or PDF, and can be scheduled and emailed to staff. An agent can collect and compile this data through software alone.
Alma can harvest COUNTER usage data through SUSHI automatically. Its built-in fulfillment dashboards cover loans, returns, requests and course reserves.

Usage data has known problems: items migrated from an old system may show only their most recent loan, and some canned reports were inaccurate. A person who knows the data still has to check the numbers before reporting to ACRL or IPEDS. Access requires staff analytics roles.

PNNL's PermitAI and SearchNEPA tools use AI to search and analyze NEPA documents. About 30 DOE evaluators are testing them, and an EIS drafting assistant and a comment-sorting tool are due in 2026. Agents can already do substantial review sub-steps, but under human oversight.

A 2025 practitioner paper describes AI in US environmental impact assessment as still at a very nascent stage. Expert biologists still have to check the ecological adequacy of reports before they are used.

Some local agencies, such as Ventura County under CEQA, accept biological work only from approved qualified biologists. That is an accountability barrier: a human must stand behind the adequacy findings.

Vendors sell AI voice agents for restaurants that answer the phone, take reservations (checking availability, party size, time and special requests) and send takeout orders straight to the POS. Unusual or large-party requests are passed to staff. These are vendor marketing claims, not independent evaluations.

Restaurant voice agents can update reservation systems and route calls to a person when needed. That covers the phone part of the task end to end, while greeting, seating and thanking guests still happen in person on the restaurant floor, which the agent cannot do.
Vendor posts describe 24/7 AI handling of restaurant phone orders and bookings. None of the sources mention a licence or legal rule requiring a human to take reservations or orders.

A patented vision system watches dining tables through existing surveillance cameras and flags plates, utensils and spills left behind. It labels each area as normal, possibly needing cleaning, or needing cleaning. This is a patent, and I found no current product for dining-room tables.

Commercial AI camera systems for restaurants, such as Dragontail, check sanitation mainly in kitchens and food-prep areas, like glove and mask use and how often surfaces are cleaned. They work only with cameras installed on site. They do not walk the floor, touch surfaces or fix table settings.

Wobot connects to a restaurant's existing CCTV and checks conditions and activities in real time. The examples it shows are mostly kitchen and counter tasks, so an agent could only help with visual checks where these cameras exist. The host still has to walk the room, look closely, touch surfaces and fix the setup.

Childcare software such as KidKare and Brightwheel already handles the digital parts of the task: CACFP-compliant menu planning, flagging missing meal components, and logging meals. Preparing and serving the food is still done by hand.
Illinois licensing rules require staff to be present to supervise children at mealtimes and require food service to be managed by a state-certified food service manager.
Ontario requires at least one trained food handler or supervisor on the premises of childcare settings that serve meals, and food handlers must meet personal hygiene requirements.

Funeral home community outreach is in-person: staffing booths at local events, handing out giveaways and collecting contact details face to face. The task's core needs physical presence and personal relationship-building.

Funeral marketing software can already schedule posts and newsletters, invite people to in-person events and send automated follow-up emails. This covers support sub-steps like promotion and follow-up, but not attending or presenting.
Brand and preneed material tools work with general AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT. That supports drafting presentation and promotional materials while a human delivers them.
Commercial AI exit-interview agents run the offboarding conversation by chat, email or voice. They adapt questions, analyse sentiment and send summaries to HR dashboards.

Offboarding automation starts checklists from HRIS termination events, generates documents such as COBRA notices, final paycheck acknowledgments and state wage notices, routes them for e-signature and files them back to the HRIS.

HR platforms and access tools each cover only about half of offboarding tasks, and coordination between functions often falls through the gaps, so a human still needs to oversee and close out the work.

The search found no product where an AI agent negotiates for a union or employer. The 2026 sources describe unions bargaining over how employers use AI, and AI used to prepare or support union work. They do not describe AI conducting the talks.
The NLRA duty to bargain in good faith includes meeting at reasonable times and places, which can be in person or by video conference. Physical presence is therefore not strictly required.
Commentary lists negotiators without real authority as a sign of bad-faith bargaining. In practice the other side expects an accountable human representative who can commit the party.

Under 49 CFR 232.103(n), unattended equipment must be secured by applying hand brakes, and railroads must have procedures to verify securement. FRA guidance defines unattended equipment by whether a qualified person can readily control its brakes.

Remote electrically driven hand brakes are still FRA prototypes and are not standard in the fleet. The FRA describes hand brakes as requiring workers to climb ladders or go between cars to operate them by hand.
Under 49 CFR 232.105(b), a locomotive's hand or parking brake must be applied and released by hand and be able to hold the unit on a 3% grade.
Canva's Magic Design builds editable event posters from a text prompt and uploaded images. Its Magic Switch feature turns one design into matching social posts and an email newsletter.
Figma Make can build nonprofit websites from a plain description of the fundraising goal and page sections, including event pages, RSVPs and volunteer signups.
Eventnook's AI builder makes event sites for charity galas and fundraising events, with registration and ticketing, from a text prompt or an uploaded design.

AI fitness tools I found, such as Virtuagym's Max AI Coach and TrueCoach-listed assistants, generate workout plans and content or check exercise form. They are built for one-to-one client coaching. I found no product that mentors or trains staff to lead group classes.
AI4Fit, a university research project, only supplies workout data to support a human coach's feedback. The trainer stays the one who gives it.

The ACSM group exercise instructor credential is a knowledge exam taken online or at a test centre, and the results showed no practical component. This suggests no licence requires a human to do the mentoring. The hands-on parts of mentoring, such as demonstrating, cueing, observing classes and correcting staff, remain physical and in person.

Ocular motility tests such as the prism cover test are done in person. The examiner holds occluders and prisms, sets fixation targets and coaches the patient, and getting a young child to cooperate is a known difficulty. A software-only agent cannot do this hands-on work.

Dedicated eye-tracking hardware, such as the University of Auckland digital cover test, can automate the measurement. These systems are separate physical devices, not general AI agents, and a 2025 review notes several barriers that keep them out of routine clinical use.

One eye-tracker system reports a nine-point comitancy screen in under two minutes. An agent could help with recording and reading the results, but a person still has to set up and run the test with the patient.

State nursing boards list specimen collection as a hands-on CNA skill: clean-catch and 24-hour urine, stool and sputum. This means being physically present with the patient and handling the containers.
Training modules describe bedside steps such as having the patient rinse their mouth before giving sputum and collecting it in the morning. These are physical, interpersonal care steps.
Robotic sputum and urine collection systems exist only as research prototypes. Automation is mainly found in lab processing after collection, not at the bedside.

CNAs pick up skin changes such as redness, swelling and bruising, and blood in urine, while giving hands-on personal care at the bedside. They report these to the supervising nurse and do not diagnose them.

A smartphone AI app that staged pressure injuries from photos reached only about 63% accuracy in validation. It also needs a human to take the picture, so the AI can only help with images someone else captures.
CNA skills are carried out under the direction and supervision of a licensed nurse.
O*NET lists 'Position or hold patients in position for surgical preparation' as a hands-on orderly/aide task done in person with the patient.
Orderlies help position patients under staff direction. This is physical handling of the patient, not work done through software or documents.
Today, surgical positioning relies on people holding limbs by hand or on mechanical positioner devices. Neither is a software or AI agent capability.
Blood-donor canteen roles involve physically serving snacks and drinks, restocking and sanitizing tables, and talking with donors face to face. Listings say mobility is needed to serve refreshments.
Canteen staff watch donors in person after donation for adverse reactions and tell staff right away. This needs someone physically present in the room.
This is often an unlicensed role done by volunteers or attendants, so there is no licensing barrier. The work is greeting donors and handing out refreshments in the refreshment area.

To make timed prints, a person loads the conformed negative on a Hazeltine analyzer, picks printer-light settings for each scene, and sends them to a contact printer. Today the timer types the corrections into a computer that the printer reads, but the film handling, printing and review are still physical.

Printer lights for each scene are set on a 1 to 50 point scale for each of red, green and blue. Automatic timing from densitometer readings has existed since 1956. Even so, a skilled timer usually needs two or three trial prints to get a balanced result.

Software tools such as Resolve's Shot Match and scene-cut detection can suggest color matches between shots. Guides say to treat the result as a starting point, not a finished grade. These tools are digital and do not run photochemical printers.

Stantec/Page describe an AI framework that speeds up early-stage energy modeling, which normally takes up to 80 hours. It is built on Honeybee/Ladybug parametric tools, so performance analysis can run inside design exploration.

A review of generative AI and optimization methods for sustainable architecture reports energy reductions of about 23-28% in studies. This suggests software can automate design-option generation and performance optimization.
A licensed architect must prepare or directly supervise building permit documents and sign, seal and date them. Plans without proper seals are returned without review.

Modular green roof trays are placed by hand on rooftops. Installers lay them over a root barrier on a sound, watertight membrane, clip them together and level them. The trays weigh about 75 kg/m² when saturated, and the plants must be installed within about 24 hours of unpacking. All of this is physical work an agent without a body cannot do. Software can only help with side work such as layout planning or load checks.
Patents for modular living roofs describe trays that sit on the roof membrane, with drainage holes and adjustable leveling devices that the installer sets on site.

Many US states and localities require a license or registration to do roofing work, so a licensed human contractor is accountable for it. California's C-39 license covers installing waterproofing surfaces. Search found no green-roof-specific licensing rule, so it is only inferred that these rules cover green roof installs.
NSW's energy-efficiency retrofit scheme says any electrical work on an air conditioner must be done by a licensed electrician, and every upgrade must meet licensing requirements.
In British Columbia, replacing or upgrading complete light fixtures in an LED retrofit generally needs an electrical permit tied to a contractor installation permit or operating permit.
AI tools help with the planning steps (finding retrofit opportunities, ranking upgrades by return, recommending lighting retrofits). The physical installation itself still needs a person on site.

Coupa says it has built more than 20 AI agents, and its 'prescriptions' combine agentic AI with mathematical optimization to assess transportation networks and warehouse capacity. A Bain executive says this cuts the work from 4-6 weeks to 4-6 hours. These figures come from the vendor and a conference talk and were not verified independently.

KPMG describes AI network optimization agents that decide how many distribution centers to have and where, set inventory for each site, and simulate what happens when a distribution center changes. These are the main sub-steps of facility and capacity planning.

Supply chain planning agent designs are moving from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop, but humans still check the assumptions and approve the results. No licence or sign-off is legally required for logistics capacity analyses. This is a general assessment, with the article available only as a paywalled excerpt.
Cleaning a kennel is hands-on work: scooping waste, washing bedding, scrubbing, applying disinfectant and letting it sit, then rinsing. Only physical presence gets it done.
Where cage cleaning is automated, it is done by physical cage-washing machines, not by software agents.
Software only helps at the edges, with things like cleaning schedules and digital checklists. That is a very small share of the task's working time.

Under NFPA 10, the monthly check is a hands-on, on-site visual inspection. It covers whether the unit is in its assigned spot, nothing blocks access, the gauge reads in range, seals are intact, weight (by weighing or hefting) and visible damage. The inspector's date and initials must be recorded on a tag, a checklist or electronically.

NFPA codes allow electronic monitoring of extinguishers (location, access, pressure) instead of the physical 30-day inspection. This only works where sensors have already been installed, so an agent could review monitoring data and logs but could not check equipment without sensors.

A vendor (Keltron) says the 2026 edition of NFPA 10 allows technology in place of monthly physical inspections. This is the vendor's own claim, and the change still depends on sensor hardware being installed.

Trade press such as Premium Beauty News and CosmeticsDesign publishes ingredient, research and trend coverage online. An agent with browsing can watch these sources and write summarized digests on its own.

Much industry learning still happens in person: trade shows (in-cosmetics Global, Paris, April 2026), hands-on treatment training and trying products on skin. An agent with no body cannot do these, and the specialist still has to absorb what is learned.

Some states require license holders to complete continuing education themselves to renew. For example, Oregon requires 5 hours a year for advanced estheticians, and self-study is allowed. Other states require none. This is a personal learning requirement, not a sign-off that an agent could do instead.

Taking off lug nuts and wheels is hands-on mechanical work. The automated systems that do it are physical robots with sockets and arms, not software agents. The reference AI agents have no body or robotics, so they cannot do this task.

A TechCrunch article from September 2026 reports that PitPro's tire-changing robot went live in Canada, aimed at commercial fleets. This is dedicated robotic hardware, which falls outside the software-only reference technology.
Bain says AI agents can track supplier performance, market shifts and supply risks in real time. This covers the KPI, delivery and spend-vs-budget monitoring sub-steps.
Industry outlooks say semi-autonomous procurement agents still need human approval for sensitive judgments such as supplier evaluations and contract recommendations.
On-site supplier visits are usually limited to critical, high-risk or sole-source vendors, and remote audits are common for lower-risk suppliers. No general legal rule requires on-site audits.

Even dedicated manicure robots (Clockwork) only paint polish: they cannot cut or shape nails, and they do not offer acrylic extensions. A software-only AI agent has no body to apply powder, solvent or nail forms at all.
No full salon-type manicure with shaping and buffing was offered by the robotic players Clockwork, Coral or Nimble.

Nebraska requires a state nail technology licence to attach, shape or adjust artificial nails using acrylic, resin, fabric or gel systems. Other states similarly require licensed nail technicians for paid acrylic services.

Rigging control cables means physically setting the controls to neutral, adjusting turnbuckles, and measuring tension with a calibrated tensiometer and the correct riser. The reading is then corrected for temperature using rigging charts and checked again after the controls are cycled. An agent could only help with the chart lookup and the temperature correction.
Tension values must be checked against the approved maintenance manual or manufacturer data for the specific model, using hand-held tensiometers such as the Tensitron units.

Under 14 CFR Part 43, only certificated persons, or people they personally supervise, may do maintenance on aircraft, and a person authorized under §43.7 must approve the aircraft for return to service. In production, a human quality inspector likewise has to sign off on flight-control rigging.
Travel CRMs already use AI to enter data from booking confirmations, and supplier integrations bring confirmation numbers, schedule changes and service updates straight into client records.

Agency software offers AI-driven CRM updates, including automatic logging of emails and calls, removing duplicates and cleaning data; vendor CRMs also track supplier rates, allotments and package quotes. These are vendor claims, not independent case studies.
California's Seller of Travel law requires the business to register (owners, trust account or bond), but no rule says a person has to do the data entry or sign each client or vendor record.

In 2026, AI scheduling agents such as Carly, Blockit and Skej are sold as tools that read email threads, negotiate times with outside participants, then book and reschedule within set rules without approval at each step. These sources are vendor blogs, so they are marketing claims, not independent tests.

Microsoft 365 Copilot in Outlook can check attendees' free/busy times, suggest time slots, book a room, draft an agenda and send invites from an email thread. It is a guided chat that the user starts. According to a competitor's comparison blog, it does not negotiate times by email on its own.

Gemini's 'Help Me Schedule' in Gmail suggests meeting times from the email thread and the user's calendar. The user starts it, and an article that may be out of date says it only works for meetings with two people.

Cloud-connected electronic shelf labels update prices straight from POS/ERP systems. This is fixed automation, not a software agent, and it covers only the price-marking part. Stores without ESLs still need someone to put tags on by hand.

Autonomous robot restocking is still a pilot as of Oct 2026. In Salling Group's Føtex trial, humanoid robots need human operators to guide every movement, and independent restocking is targeted for early 2027. Either way, robots fall outside the no-body reference technology.
Shelf-scanning systems such as Simbe's find gaps and pricing errors, but store staff still do the physical restocking. The work requires someone in the store moving goods by hand.

Farm inventory software already tracks feed use, sends reorder-point alerts and drafts purchase orders for the user to approve. Bin-level sensor systems such as BinMaster FeedView automate feed inventory tracking and online ordering. This covers the monitoring, comparison and ordering steps but not receiving or putting stock away.

BinMaster FeedView combines wireless laser bin-level sensors with cloud software that forecasts feed use and supports online ordering. Without such sensors, someone has to check stock levels in person.

In the US, medically important antibiotics for livestock (in feed, water, injectables and boluses) can only be bought with a veterinary feed directive (VFD) or prescription from a licensed vet under a vet-client-patient relationship. The vet authorizes the drug, but the buyer does not need a license to place the order.

AlertMedia's AI Plan Builder (August 2026) lets security teams generate response plans from a natural-language prompt and check current regulations, with users reviewing or reverting the AI's changes. This shows plan drafting can be largely delegated but still goes through human review.
Swimlane's investigation agent uses the NIST incident response framework and the customer's own runbooks to produce a prioritized plan covering containment, eradication, recovery and hardening.

NIST SP 800-61r3 (aligned with CSF 2.0) is guidance, not law. It calls for defined roles and escalation authority but does not require a licensed human to write or sign the plan. Approval is an organizational governance step, not a legal one.

Vendor sources (to be read with caution) say AI agents in 2026 automate month-end narratives and risk-memo drafting and can produce a full first-draft management pack. A human still signs off on the numbers, and the CFO typically reviews the pack.

Microsoft's release plan says Copilot for Finance can run variance analysis in Excel against ERP data (Dynamics 365, SAP) and produce reports with comments for stakeholders. Users review and adjust the results, and Microsoft's own estimate is 30% faster reporting. The feature entered public preview in June 2025, and its current availability was not confirmed.
Agents can model the impact when assumptions change, find ways to reduce risk, and alert stakeholders. A human still checks the figures before they are used.

Making the case for warehouse automation capex is a standard desk analysis: define the scope (volumes, WMS/WCS interfaces, building and power work), then calculate payback, NPV and IRR against WACC. An agent with code execution and web access can do this from operational data and vendor quotes.

Companies usually approve capex through a delegation-of-authority matrix. Named roles have monetary limits, and large purchases go to the board. Approver roles are kept separate from initiators, so a person with that authority must sign off.

Delegation-of-authority approvals are increasingly built into ERP workflows such as SAP S/4HANA. Software sends the request through, but the approval itself still comes from a human who holds the authority.

Vendors sell investment-analyst AI agents that run screens, pull filings and transcripts, summarize earnings, refresh models and draft coverage notes end to end. Analysts still review the output, and live agentic deployments remain early-stage.

Multi-agent equity research setups (document analyzer, model-building analyst agent, a portfolio-manager agent that challenges the thesis) are described for producing investment theses. The post is promotional and gives no outcome data.

In the US, research analysts who publish recommendations must hold FINRA Research Analyst registration (SIE plus Series 86/87), so a registered human has to be accountable for and approve published recommendations.

Maritime predictive-maintenance tools connect to planned maintenance systems and can create work orders and schedule maintenance around voyages and port calls. They do not handle the hands-on repair, and they say little about dispatching repairs, spares or shipyards.
Planned, predictive and breakdown maintenance of ship machinery is done to classification society rules (e.g. Lloyd's) and flag state law, under the responsibility of the engineers on board.
Under survey requirements and the ISM Code, maintenance and repair records must be completed and engine room logs signed by the chief engineer, so a human has to sign off.

Current DJ software handles stem separation, BPM matching and transitions. Commentators from 2025 and 2026 say that reading a live crowd is still done by human DJs. The webcam 'crowd-reading' features are an April Fool's joke, not real products.
djOS (April 2026) is presented as an AI co-pilot that plugs into DJ platforms and responds to the crowd. It is a press release only, and I found no proof that it works on its own in real venues.
Public performance licenses (ASCAP/BMI/SESAC) are usually held by the venue. No law requires a person to be the one who selects or plays the music.
AI voice agents sold in 2026 answer clinic calls and book visits straight into clinic calendars or scheduling systems, and pass complex cases to staff.
Vendors say AI scheduling agents write bookings into EHRs through HL7/FHIR standards and native connectors, for example NextGen. This is a vendor claim.
A vendor guide on AI scheduling agents deployed by health systems reports an 89% drop in call abandonment at one system. This result has not been independently checked.

AI registry products already automate case finding, abstraction and NAACCR-format reporting from clinical data. Vendors report cutting per-case abstraction from about 2 hours to 10–20 minutes, with human validation still in the loop. These are vendor claims.

Statistical analysis of registry data runs on standard software (NCI SEER*Stat, SEER*DMS, CDC EDITS). An agent with code execution can drive tools like these to produce tables, charts and narrative summaries.

The credentialing rules found (CTR requirements from CoC and state registries) cover abstraction and registry staff, not who prepares statistical reports. Registrars prepare and submit reports to SEER/NCDB under those standards, so in practice a human still reviews and is accountable for the work.

Firefighters reach the seat of the fire by physically stretching and advancing hose lines inside burning buildings. Crews read the flow path, stairwells and building layout on the spot, so the core of the task is bodily movement under IDLH conditions.

AI navigation aids for firefighters (deep-learning thermal imaging with AR overlays) are still mostly academic prototypes. They only advise the firefighter, who still does all the moving, and are not standard tools.

Fire department operating guidelines put interior attack and entry decisions in the hands of trained, certified crews and officers on the fireground. A software agent has no body and could at most do pre-incident building lookups.

Automatic pump pressure governors are built into pumper apparatus, not run by general-purpose AI agents. They hold the discharge pressure the operator sets by adjusting engine speed. The operator still engages the pump, sets the pressure and watches for cavitation at the panel on the truck.
Newer integrated pump panels such as REV Smart Flo cut pump engagement down to a button press. The controls are on the apparatus and a person has to operate them there.

Under NFPA 1002, pump operators must hold Driver/Operator–Pumper certification. That requires Firefighter I, written and hands-on practical exams on the apparatus, a medical evaluation and a driver's license.

Casino workforce software such as UKG Virtual Roster automatically matches staff to shifts by skill and handles labor-demand forecasting, union rules, labor laws and internal policies. This means the scheduling part of the task can be delegated end to end.

New Jersey requires anyone with supervisory responsibility over casino areas, such as a pit boss or shift manager, to hold a casino key employee license before starting work. Supervisory authority therefore has to sit with a licensed human.
Washington's rules require a licensed floor supervisor for each gambling area. Supervising and evaluating dealers on the floor means being there in person.

Retort controls already run temperature and timing through a fully automatic cremation cycle, and some systems allow off-site monitoring and alarms over the internet. Loading the body, opening the door and removing the remains are still done by hand, so software could at most help monitor the cycle and keep records.
Virginia requires anyone operating a crematory retort to hold CANA, ICCFA or another board-recognised certification, and trainees must work under a certified operator.
In South Carolina, a person may not perform cremations before receiving a Crematory Operator Registration, and the crematory must remove all remains from the retort at the end of each cremation.

Vendor comparisons for 2026 list AI agents that generate invoices and run billing, collections and cash application from start to finish. They say these agents check outgoing invoices against customer records and past invoices. These figures come from vendors and have not been independently checked.

Agentic AP/AR platforms in 2026 claim 70-90% of invoices go through with no human touch at scale. This suggests the main sub-steps are already automated, though McKinsey reports that only about 6% of finance functions have scaled AI.

E-invoicing rules usually ask for a digital or qualified electronic signature tied to the issuer, not a human's handwritten one. India, for example, drops the signature requirement for e-invoices, so the law does not require a person to issue each invoice.

Camera-based AI that detects missing PPE and people in risk zones exists, but the agribusiness deployment found used existing CCTV in fixed grain-handling areas. The vineyard field study was only a preliminary image-based study, and no forestry tools turned up. That means open-field, remote crews mostly have no camera coverage an agent could watch.

Under OSHA, the employer that directs and controls the workers is responsible for their safety. That employer must get workers to comply and can discipline them, and fines fall on the employer, not the employee.

A model logging safety program requires a competent supervisor on each jobsite with authority to enforce the safety program. Violations can lead to discipline or termination, so a human with on-site authority is expected to give warnings and discipline.

Under EPA's Worker Protection Standard, pesticide safety training must use EPA-approved materials. It must be given by a qualified trainer, such as a certified applicator or someone who completed an EPA-approved train-the-trainer course, before workers enter treated areas and again every 12 months. Records must be kept for 2 years.
The EPA's training checklists cover worker and handler topics, including the Application Exclusion Zone. The delivery format is a person presenting to workers, not standalone software.

AI video tools such as HeyGen and Miraflow can generate multilingual farm safety and crop-management training videos. This covers the materials-preparation part of the task, but not the hands-on field demonstration of planting, harvesting or insect identification.

Farm scheduling products such as FieldClock already do job-based crew scheduling and piece-rate tracking. One 2026 review says FieldClock's schedule shows the work but not which worker is doing it, and it sends no notices when plans change, so a person still assigns crews and passes on changes.
Vendors are marketing AI agents that catch crew and equipment conflicts across several fields. The figures they publish look like demo output, not measured results.

Good farm scheduling has to account for weather, crop growth stages and whether equipment is available. That information often comes from what the supervisor sees in the field and from talking with crew leads, not from systems an agent can reach.

Vendors say drone and computer-vision software can find anomalies and assess damage in imagery, but a person or robot has to capture the imagery on site first. The agent only analyzes what it is given.

One pre-seed startup builds drone and software systems that analyze aerial images of farms and infrastructure. This is narrow vendor tooling, not a general agent that can walk through barns, grain bins, irrigation systems or equipment.

AI drone inspections can flag problems in infrastructure, but the evidence comes from vendor and industry-blog material without independent accuracy checks. For farm buildings, a human still has to look, touch and test things in person.
Bunching flowers is automated only by dedicated hardware, not by software AI agents. Bercomex sells machines that cut, count, bunch and bind stems.
Bercomex says its Furora Nova line sorts and bunches cut flowers fully automatically using a physical processing line. This automation depends on robotics and machinery, not on a software agent.
Packing bouquets into boxes, including taping or wrapping the stems, needs physical equipment such as conveyors, drop mechanisms and taping machines, as described in a US patent.

Software such as onX Hunt only supports the trip. It offers offline GPS maps, land-ownership layers, trails, waypoints and track recording, but a human still has to walk, drive, boat or ski to the hunting area.
onX navigation (GPS, compass mode, tracker) assists a hunter who is physically travelling through unfamiliar terrain, so the help is limited to planning and wayfinding.

Phone apps can download offline maps up to about 150 miles wide for areas with no coverage, but they don't move the person. The task itself is physical travel by foot, vehicle, boat, snowmobile or skis.

O*NET lists 'Maintain engines, fishing gear, and other on-board equipment and perform minor repairs' as a core task of Fishing and Hunting Workers. Career guides say it covers hands-on work such as mending nets, replacing lines and doing basic engine checks on board.

AI marine engine diagnostic and predictive-maintenance tools exist, such as ioCurrents MarineInsight and Yanmar SHIPSWEB. They flag faults and suggest maintenance from sensor data, but they need onboard data connections and crew to do the physical repairs.
Yanmar SHIPSWEB offers chatbot help and engine diagnosis for vessels, which supports troubleshooting, not the repair itself.

Garmin chartplotters already plan routes automatically. Auto Guidance builds a path from vessel settings and chart data, and a connected autopilot can follow it. Garmin warns that this does not ensure clearance from obstacles or the bottom, so a human still has to check the route.

Under the STCW-F Convention, every officer in charge of a navigational watch on a fishing vessel of 24 m or more in unlimited waters must hold a certificate. The skipper must ensure the watch arrangements are safe. Legal responsibility for navigation therefore stays with a certified human on board.
STCW-F is the IMO treaty that sets certification and training standards for crews of seagoing fishing vessels. The Code was revised by Resolution MSC.562(108) in 2024.

To transfer an animal, the trapper lines up a sliding-door transfer cage with the trap's release door, pulls the door up, then closes and latches it once the animal has moved across. This is all physical handling.
Releasing or handling trapped animals means wearing heavy gloves, covering the cage, and holding or carrying the animal, so someone has to be there in person.
Guidance for birds caught in multi-catch cages has the handler go into the cage with gloves and a towel, then hold the bird by its body and legs to release it.

An Alaska state description of fishing deckhand work says deckhands attach nets, slings, hooks and other lifting devices to cables, booms and hoists. They load equipment and supplies by hand or with hoisting equipment and signal coworkers to position the loads. All of this is physical work on the vessel.

Seasonal fishing job postings from the U.S. Department of Labor list loading and unloading equipment, catch and supplies at the start and end of each day. The work includes attaching gear to the cable, boom and hoist and lifting up to 100 lb.

A crab deckhand posting includes loading and unloading supplies and offloading product among the duties. It says some boats may require crane operator certification, and gear such as crab pots can weigh 850-1150 lb. No software can stand in for this hands-on handling. The most an agent could add is small planning help, such as supply checklists.

Scan tools now include AI assistants, such as TEXA IDC6 AI Smart Diagnosis. They walk the technician through each diagnostic step and suggest repair paths from validated case data and technical service bulletins (TSBs), but the technician still connects the tool and carries out the tests. This is augmentation, not autonomous troubleshooting.

Bosch is adding a conversational AI assistant to ESI[tronic], previewed for 2026 with rollout in release 2026/4. It cross-checks live vehicle diagnostic data against OEM repair information and Bosch's experience-based repair database. It helps with interpretation, while the physical measurements stay with the technician.

The federal EPA technician certification found (Section 609) covers motor-vehicle A/C service, not fuel, ignition or emissions troubleshooting. State smog-repair licensing was not checked, so a human sign-off requirement is not established for typical diagnostic work.

The task is hands-on. A worker has to physically mount the compressor and condenser on frames using hand tools and acetylene welding or brazing equipment. A software-only agent with no robotics cannot do this. At most it could look up specs or mounting diagrams, which is a very small share of the time.

In the US, anyone who installs, maintains, services or repairs equipment containing regulated refrigerant must hold EPA Section 608 technician certification. This works as the main occupational licence for HVAC technicians.

To get Section 608 certification, a technician must pass an EPA-approved test given by an approved certifying organization. Installation work on refrigerant-containing systems falls under this requirement.

Patching a plaster mold is all hands-on work: roughen the damaged spot, wet it, mix the plaster to a paste, press it onto chipped edges, let it dry and sand it smooth. An agent with no robotics can't do any of these steps.
Repairing chips and cracks in plaster means applying and shaping setting compounds by hand in layers, letting each dry and sanding between them. No software can do this.
Guidance on chipped edges and corners covers stiff setting materials, the right consistency and drying between layers. These are manual skills, and an AI could only help by looking up instructions.

Transfinder's Wayfinder driver app is tied to its Routefinder PLUS routing software and gives school bus drivers turn-by-turn directions with voice guidance on a tablet. Edulog's tablets do the same with Edulog Routing and Planning. This software can take over most of the map-reading and route interpretation, but it only helps the driver.

Under federal rules, every school bus driver must hold a CDL with passenger and school bus (S) endorsements. That means the person following the route behind the wheel has to be a licensed human, since the agent has no body and cannot drive the bus.
Vendors sell school-specific turn-by-turn navigation for drivers. The driver still has to physically follow the directions while driving and deal with verbal changes from dispatch.

Yard inventory systems such as RailComm/Tracsis iTrack already keep a live railcar count automatically, using AEI readers, cameras and turnout sensors, and compare it with the car management system's records. An agent working through these systems could compile counts of available cars and cars sent to repair.

Under 49 CFR 215.9, a qualified person must physically find and tag defective (bad-order) cars before they move to repair. So someone has to be in the yard to identify cars and the type of service each needs before the numbers can be recorded.

Bad-order tag records can be electronic and must be kept for 90 days. The recordkeeping itself does not have to be done by a licensed human, though the tag carries the reporting person's signature or electronic ID.
Software for fueling crews only works out uplift quantities, converts units and logs meter tickets. The hose connection, bonding, nozzle handling and monitoring are all done by hand.
FAA AC 150/5230-4C treats line-service and supervisory fueling training under 14 CFR 139.321(e) as critical to safety. It assumes trained people do the fueling.
Fueling data is captured on rugged tablets at the point of fueling, which only digitizes the paperwork around the physical job.

Commercial cargo inspection tools such as OxMaint and Cargosnap say they record freight condition from photos taken at loading and unloading. They add timestamps and GPS, flag new damage automatically and link the record to the shipment. These are vendor claims with no independent benchmarks. Someone still has to be at the freight to take the photos or set up the cameras.

Mobile freight inspection platforms produce audit-ready photo records with timestamps and GPS. An agent could turn this evidence, plus the inspector's notes or voice memos, into a structured report, but a person on site has to collect the evidence.

US federal rules on vehicle inspection reports (49 CFR 396.11 and 396.13) require signatures from drivers and carrier officials for defects and repair certifications. They do not stop a human inspector from having an AI draft the record of freight condition and handling.

Payroll platforms such as Gusto, QuickBooks and ADP already work out and e-file Form 941 and state and local payroll tax forms automatically each time payroll runs. Filing APIs also generate, validate, e-sign and send 94x forms to the IRS, so the preparation and transmission steps are already automated.
TaxBandits offers an API that automates 94x filings from start to finish: it generates, validates, e-signs and transmits the forms.

Form 941 has to be signed under penalty of perjury by the employer or by a Reporting Agent the taxpayer has authorized on Form 8655, which the taxpayer signs. The IRS generally rejects unsigned 94x returns, so an accountable human or firm must authorize and sign the return.
